standards.name: MiAIRR (Minimal Information about an Adaptive Immune Receptor Repertoire)
standards.abstract: MiAIRR specifies metadata for adaptive immune receptor repertoire sequencing (AIRR-seq) studies. The research objects are B- and T-cell receptor repertoires profiled by high-throughput sequencing and associated sample, subject, and experimental metadata; data modalities include raw NGS reads, processed rearrangement records, and associated annotations. The standard is maintained by the AIRR Community (Minimal Standards Working Group/AIRR Community) and defines six high-level data sets (Study/Subject/Diagnosis, Sample Collection, Sample Processing and Sequencing, Raw Sequences, Data Processing, Processed AIRR Sequences with Annotations). It provides a tabular list of named metadata fields, concrete data types/formats (string, ontology term, boolean, time-interval, arrays, etc.), requirement levels (essential/important/defined), and definitions/examples to support reproducible deposition and interoperable data sharing.

classification.rationale: The source material provides a downloadable TSV/list-table of named data elements with explicit 'Field', 'Type/Format', 'Level', 'Definition', and 'Example' columns (MiAIRR Data Elements TSV). Each row names a discrete metadata field and gives a concrete data type/format, so the structure is a metadata table rather than prose guidance or a procedural DAG.

standards.standard_id: AIRR Data Schema / AIRR Data Model
standards.name: AIRR Data Schema (AIRR Data Model)
standards.abstract: The AIRR Data Schema describes metadata and data objects for adaptive immune receptor repertoire sequencing (AIRR-seq) studies, covering study/subject/sample metadata, laboratory and sequencing conditions, data processing provenance, and sequence-level annotations (Rearrangements). The specification is published and maintained by the AIRR Community as versioned schema documents (machine-readable YAML/JSON following OpenAPI v2), and it addresses interoperability and reusability by defining object schemas, field names, data types, controlled vocabularies/ontologies, and file formats for exchanging AIRR-seq datasets across tools and repositories.

classification.rationale: The source material presents concrete, field-level schema definitions and explicit tabular descriptions for schema objects and fields (e.g., 'Repertoire', 'Study', 'Subject', and many per-object TSV-like field lists). The documentation states: "The schema defines the data model, field names, data types, and encodings for AIRR standard objects." and includes many downloadable/inline tables (e.g., Repertoire TSV, Study TSV) listing named fields with types and definitions, so the source is genuinely a TABLE-style specification.

Study.name: Study
Study.descr: Information about the experimental study design, including the title of the study, laboratory contact information, funding, and linked publications.
Study.evidence: Information about the experimental study design, including the title of the study, laboratory contact information, funding, and linked publications.

Subject.name: Subject
Subject.descr: Information about the study cohorts and individual subjects, including species, sex, age, and ancestry.
Subject.evidence: Information about the study cohorts and individual subjects, including species, sex, age, and ancestry.

Diagnosis.name: Diagnosis
Diagnosis.descr: Information about disease state(s), therapies, and study group membership (e.g., control versus disease).
Diagnosis.evidence: Information about disease state(s), therapies, and study group membership (e.g., control versus disease).

Sample.name: Sample
Sample.descr: Information about the origin and expected composition of the biological sample(s). This set aims to capture essential information about the collection of a sample, including its source (e.g., anatomical site), its provenance (provider), and the experimental condition (e.g., the time point during the course of a disease or treatment).
Sample.evidence: Information about the origin and expected composition of the biological sample(s). This set aims to capture essential information about the collection of a sample, including its source (e.g., anatomical site), its provenance (provider), and the experimental condition (e.g., the time point during the course of a disease or treatment).

CellProcessing.name: CellProcessing
CellProcessing.descr: Information about the cell subset being profiled, as defined by the investigator, and the flow cytometry or other markers used to select the subset. Additional information includes the number of cells per sample and whether cells were prepared in bulk or captured as single cells.
CellProcessing.evidence: Information about the cell subset being profiled, as defined by the investigator, and the flow cytometry or other markers used to select the subset. Additional information includes the number of cells per sample and whether cells were prepared in bulk or captured as single cells.

NucleicAcidProcessing.descr: Information about nucleic acid sample type (e.g., RNA versus DNA) and how immune-receptor gene rearrangements were amplified and sequenced (for example, RACE-PCR versus multiplex PCR, paired PCR, and/or varying read length and sequencing chemistries).

SequencingRun.descr: Information about the sequencing run, such as the number of reads, read lengths, quality control parameters, the sequencing kit and instrument(s) used, and run batch number. Also includes information about the raw data for the sequencing run (e.g., FASTQ files).

standards.name: AIRR Rearrangement Schema (AIRR Formats / Data Representation)
standards.abstract: The standard covers annotated adaptive immune receptor rearrangements (e.g., antibody heavy chains, TCR beta chains) produced by AIRR-seq / Rep-Seq experiments. Recorded data are represented as tab-delimited (TSV) rows where each row is a Rearrangement object (a single rearranged receptor sequence) with many annotations including gene calls, junction sequences, alignment/CIGAR strings, positional coordinates, and quality/duplicate counts. The AIRR Data Representation Working Group (AIRR Community) maintains the schema and associated file-format specification and libraries; the standard addresses interoperability and reusability of AIRR-seq data by specifying column names, allowed data types, encoding, TSV dialect, and alignment/CIGAR conventions to facilitate machine-readable sharing across tools and repositories.

classification.rationale: The source provides a concrete tab-delimited file specification with named column headings, explicit data types, required columns, and detailed per-field examples (TSV/column-oriented schema). The material defines file/column semantics (header, required columns, allowed data types, boolean encodings, and field examples) — i.e., a genuine metadata table schema rather than prose instructions or a procedural DAG.

standards.name: AIRR Data Commons API (ADC API)
standards.abstract: The AIRR Data Commons API (ADC API) describes a programmatic interface for querying and retrieving processed AIRR-seq (adaptive immune receptor repertoire sequencing) datasets and associated metadata (repertoires and rearrangements). The research objects are immune-repertoire sequencing data and their annotations (rearrangements, repertoire/sample metadata), typically stored in distributed repositories that implement the AIRR Community standards. The ADC API is maintained by the AIRR Community (AIRR Common Repository Working Group) and defines a RESTful, JSON-based OpenAPI specification, endpoint model (notably /repertoire and /rearrangement), a query/filter language and response formats (JSON/TSV). It addresses programmatic discovery, query, and standardized return of AIRR-seq metadata across a network of repositories (the AIRR Data Commons), while allowing repositories to retain different backend implementations and to decide repository-specific defaults (e.g., which pipeline result to return by default).

classification.rationale: The source material is primarily prose guidance and a set of design/decision items (numbered decisions, meeting minutes, and descriptive text) specifying API design choices, endpoints, and behavioral recommendations. It does not present a field-level metadata table nor a sequential process DAG; rather it enumerates requirements and decisions, so 'principle' best matches the source's structure.

principles.principle: Use a RESTful, JSON API specified with OpenAPI.
principles.evidence: RESTful API, JSON, using the OpenAPI specification. Initial implementation in Github

principles.principle: Provide two primary endpoints: /repertoire (sample repertoire objects with study metadata) and /rearrangement (rearrangement objects with sequence annotations).
principles.evidence:
Two primary endpoints (“gettable” objects with unique ids)

```
/repertoire
```

The /repertoire endpoint returns a list of “sample repertoire objects” with associated study metadata. A sample repertoire object is the description (the metadata) of the biological sample, including the processing that is applied to that sample, that is sequenced and annotated to acquire a set of rearrangements from the sample's immune repertoire.

```
/rearrangement
```

The /rearrangement endpoint returns a list of “rearrangement objects” with associated annotations. A rearrangement object is associated with a sample repertoire by the repertoire’s unique id. A rearrangement object contains the annotation information for each sequence read, including the V, D, and J gene assignments, the Junction (CDR3 and conserved Amino Acids), as well as other relevant annotation information.

principles.principle: Adopt capabilities modeled on the GDC API: expressive query language, ability for clients to request specific fields, prefixed linked-entity querying, facets for aggregation, JSON/TSV return formats, and an API mapping/discovery mechanism.
principles.evidence:
The GDC API looks to be a good specification to build upon

```
https://docs.gdc.cancer.gov/API/Users_Guide/Search_and_Retrieval/
```

* It has a well-defined and expressive query language

* Clients can limit/request what data fields to be returned (versus all data being returned)

* It has a “loose” data model, which just indicates which entities are “linked” through an endpoint and can thus be queried upon, without specifying how that link is implemented. For example, the “case” endpoint is linked to the “diagnosis” entity, so a query can be performed on diagnosis data by having “diagnosis.” as a prefix to the field name, such as “diagnosis.state”.

* It has a “facets” parameter which requests a limited form of aggregation capability, specifically for driving summary graphics (pie charts, bar plots, etc.) on a web interface.

* JSON and TSV formats for return data.

* It has a “_mapping” endpoint which is a discovery mechanism which provides metadata about the API itself. We probably need to expand upon it.

principles.principle: Specify relationships between entities in the API data model but allow repositories to use different backend implementations and map those back to the API model.
principles.evidence: We will specify relationships between entities in the API data model, but each repository can have a different backend data model, which they will need to map to the API data model.

principles.principle: Define the data return formats/flattening behavior: JSON responses should be not-flattened; TSV responses should be provided for rearrangement and repertoire with stated flattening rules.
principles.evidence:
Data for return will be:

* Not-flatten, JSON response
* TSV response for /rearrangement, not-flatten, only get rearrangement data
* TSV response for /repertoire, one row for each repertoire id, flatten all study metadata

principles.principle: AIRR Data Commons repositories must both adhere to AIRR Common Repositories Working Group recommendations and implement the ADC API to be part of the AIRR Data Commons.
principles.evidence:
The AIRR Data Commons is a network of distributed repositories that store AIRR-seq data and adhere to the AIRR Community standards. We define the AIRR Data Commons as consisting of the set of repositories that both:
Adhere to the
AIRR Common Repositories Working Group recommendations
for promoting, sharing, and use of AIRR-seq data.
Implement the
ADC API
as a programmatic mechanism to access that data.

principles.principle: Do not require repositories to implement asynchronous queries, but define an asynchronous query interface for those that wish to support it.
principles.evidence: Defining an asynchronous query mode would be useful but it places a larger burden (computational and infrastructure overhead) on the repository over a simple synchronous query mode. Therefore, we will not require repositories to support it. We will define the asynchronous query mode interface.

principles.principle: Require INSDC accession numbers (e.g., BioProject, BioSample, SRA) when available to help detect duplicate datasets across repositories; do not attempt to enforce global unique IDs centrally.
principles.evidence: Conclusion: it’s challenging to enforce a globally unique ID, so CRWG API will require that INSDC accession numbers (e.g., Bioproject, Biosample, SRA) are provided so users can check for duplicates. If those accession numbers aren’t available for a specific study, the user will have to rely upon manually reviewing titles, publications, abstract, etc.

principles.principle: Allow multiple analytical pipelines' outputs for the same raw data but have each repository choose a default to return; the API should specify which fields indicate alternative pipeline results.
principles.evidence:
The same raw data may be processed through multiple analytical pipelines, (e.g., for comparative purposes) with results from all pipelines in the repository. How do we indicate this and coordinate what gets returned?

Conclusion: each repository will return only one as the default, but each repository will determine its own default. CRWG API will specify the fields that get returned to alert the user that there are alternatives.

principles.principle: Prioritize standardizing key repeating elements for computational precision: donor species, donor health status, tissue type, cell subset, sequence type, gene usage, CDR3 sequence, receptor specificity, etc.
principles.evidence:
Key repeating elements to prioritize for computationally precise standardization
* Donor species (e.g., homo sapiens) (subject)
* Donor health status (e.g., diabetes) (subject, primary sample)
* Tissue type (e.g. PBMC) (primary sample)
* Cell subset (e.g. T-cell)
* Sequence type (e.g., TRB) (also from primer selection - experimental protocol)
* Gene usage (e.g., IGHV1-69)
* CDR3 sequence ( e.g., “CASSYIKLN”)
* Receptor specificity (e.g., HIV virus)

standards.notes: Classification chosen as 'principle' because the source is a decision list and prose guidance about API design and repository behavior rather than a field-level metadata table or an ordered process DAG.
